hints: Think about what type of catalyst is needed to generate a carbocation from a chloroalkane in electrophilic substitution, recall the catalyst used with chloromethane or bromoethane.
walkthrough:
Spot the Friedel-Crafts step**
You have benzene plus $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{Cl}$ giving ethylbenzene. This is Friedel-Crafts alkylation. The real electrophile is not the chloroalkane itself, it is the carbocation $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5^+$.

Bring in the Lewis acid**
The $\text{C-Cl}$ bond is polar but does not break on its own. A strong Lewis acid such as $\text{AlCl}_3$ (or $\text{FeCl}_3$) accepts the chloride lone pair, polarises the bond to breaking point and takes $\text{Cl}^-$ away as $\text{AlCl}_4^-$, leaving $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5^+$ free to attack the benzene ring.
Final answer: $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{Cl} + \text{AlCl}_3 \rightarrow \text{C}_2\text{H}_5^+ + \text{AlCl}_4^-$

hints: Recall what the numbers 1,2 and 1,4 mean on a benzene ring, think adjacent carbons versus opposite carbons.
walkthrough:
Draw the common backbone**
Start with a regular hexagon with a circle inside for benzene in both boxes. The substituent in both cases is ethyl, $\text{-CH}_2\text{CH}_3$.

Place the groups correctly**
For 1,2, put the two $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5$ groups on two neighbouring carbons, side by side. For 1,4, put them on carbons directly across the ring from each other, with two ring carbons between them on each side.

Final answer: 1,2-diethylbenzene: benzene ring with two $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5$ groups on adjacent carbons (ortho). 1,4-diethylbenzene: benzene ring with two $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5$ groups on opposite carbons (para).

hints: Think about the ethyl group already on ethylbenzene, is it electron donating or electron withdrawing, and which positions does that type of group direct to.
walkthrough:
Remember the directing power of alkyl**
An alkyl group like $\text{-C}_2\text{H}_5$ pushes electron density toward the ring by the positive inductive effect. It activates the ring and directs incoming electrophiles to the 2, 4 and 6 positions, which are ortho and para to itself.

Link to the observed products**
Attack at position 2 gives 1,2-diethylbenzene and attack at position 4 gives 1,4-diethylbenzene. Position 3 is meta to the ethyl group and is not activated, so 1,3-diethylbenzene hardly forms.
Final answer: Ethyl group is electron donating by positive inductive effect and is 2,4-directing, so substitution occurs at ortho (2) and para (4) positions, giving very little 1,3 (meta) product.

hints: Recall which strong oxidant converts alkyl side chains on benzene completely to $\text{-COOH}$, think purple solution used hot and alkaline then acidified.
walkthrough:
Recognise complete side-chain oxidation**
Both ethyl groups are oxidised right down to carboxylic acid groups while the benzene ring survives. This vigorous oxidation needs hot concentrated $\text{KMnO}_4$ in alkaline conditions, then acidification to get the free $\text{-COOH}$ acid.
Final answer: Hot alkaline $\text{KMnO}_4$ / $\text{MnO}_4^-$, followed by dilute acid.

hints: Write the formula of 1,2-diethylbenzene as $\text{C}_{10}\text{H}_{14}$ and note the statement that all atoms in the two ethyl groups except those becoming $\text{COOH}$ carbons end up as $\text{CO}_2$ and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$.
Balance C, then H, then O by adjusting the number of [O] atoms, check that $\text{C}_6\text{H}_4(\text{COOH})_2$ contains $\text{C}_8\text{H}_6\text{O}_4$.
walkthrough:
Set up the skeleton**
1,2-diethylbenzene is $\text{C}_6\text{H}_4(\text{C}_2\text{H}_5)_2$, which is $\text{C}_{10}\text{H}_{14}$. The product $\text{C}_6\text{H}_4(\text{COOH})_2$ keeps 8 carbons, so the other 2 carbons from the ethyl groups must appear as $2\text{CO}_2$. Hydrogen left over appears as $\text{H}_2\text{O}$.

Balance to find [O]**
Count atoms: products contain $8 + 2 = 10$ C, $6 + 8 = 14$ H, $4 + 4 + 4 = 12$ O. Reactant hydrocarbon supplies C and H, so all 12 O must come from $12[\text{O}]$. That gives $$\text{C}_{10}\text{H}_{14} + 12[\text{O}] \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_4(\text{COOH})_2 + 2\text{CO}_2 + 4\text{H}_2\text{O}$$

hints: Look for symmetry in benzene-1,2-dioic acid, decide which ring carbons are equivalent and whether the two $\text{COOH}$ carbons are equivalent.
walkthrough:
Count unique carbon environments**
Benzene-1,2-dioic acid has a plane of symmetry through the middle of the $\text{C}1-\text{C}2$ bond and the $\text{C}4-\text{C}5$ bond. So $\text{C}1 = \text{C}2$, $\text{C}3 = \text{C}6$, $\text{C}4 = \text{C}5$, and the two $\text{C=O}$ carbons are identical. That is 3 ring environments plus 1 carbonyl environment, giving 4 peaks in total.
Final answer: 4 peaks.

hints: Compare $\text{CHCl}_3$ and $\text{CDCl}_3$, think which nucleus each contains and which one would give a signal in a proton spectrum.
walkthrough:
Why deuterate the solvent**
Proton NMR detects $^1\text{H}$. Ordinary $\text{CHCl}_3$ has a proton and would produce its own large peak that could hide sample peaks. $\text{CDCl}_3$ has D ($^2\text{H}$) instead of H, so it is invisible in the $^1\text{H}$ spectrum.
Final answer: $\text{CDCl}_3$ contains no $^1\text{H}$ so gives no peak and does not interfere with the spectrum, whereas $\text{CHCl}_3$ would give a proton peak.

hints: Compare Fig. 6.1 and Fig. 6.2, decide which one shows alkyl signals near $\delta$ 1 to 3 plus an aromatic signal, matching ethylbenzene.
Recall the n+1 rule, a proton with n equivalent neighbours on the adjacent carbon is split into n+1 peaks.
Apply this to $\text{-CH}_2\text{CH}_3$, work out how many neighbours the $\text{CH}_3$ protons see and how many the $\text{CH}_2$ protons see.
walkthrough:
Identify Fig. 6.1 as ethylbenzene**
Fig. 6.1 shows three regions: a multiplet near $\delta$ 7.2 for the aromatic ring, a signal near $\delta$ 2.6 and a signal near $\delta$ 1.2 for aliphatic protons. That fits $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$. Fig. 6.2 with only two singlets, one very downfield at 13.1, fits the dioic acid.

Explain the triplet at 1.2**
The $\delta$ 1.2 peak is the $\text{CH}_3$ group. Its protons are next to $\text{CH}_2$ with 2 equivalent protons. By the n+1 rule, $2 + 1 = 3$, so a triplet is seen.

Explain the quartet at 2.6**
The $\delta$ 2.6 peak is the benzylic $\text{CH}_2$ group, deshielded by the ring. It is next to $\text{CH}_3$ with 3 equivalent protons. By the n+1 rule, $3 + 1 = 4$, so a quartet is seen.

Final answer: substance: ethylbenzene, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{C}_2\text{H}_5$.
peak at $\delta = 1.2$: triplet, $\text{CH}_3$, split by 2H on neighbouring $\text{CH}_2$.
peak at $\delta = 2.6$: quartet, $\text{CH}_2$, split by 3H on neighbouring $\text{CH}_3$.

hints: Look at Fig. 6.2 with peaks at $\delta$ 7.8 and 13.1, think which proton appears very downfield near 11 to 14 and which appears in the aromatic region.
walkthrough:
Assign the two singlets**
The peak at $\delta$ 7.8 is in the aromatic region 7 to 8, so it is the four ring protons of $\text{C}_6\text{H}_4$. The broad peak at $\delta$ 13.1 is highly deshielded, characteristic of the hydrogen bonded $\text{-COOH}$ proton. No splitting is seen because there are no protons on adjacent atoms in either case.

Final answer: substance: benzene-1,2-dioic acid, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_4(\text{COOH})_2$.
peak at $\delta = 7.8$: H on benzene ring / $\text{C}_6\text{H}_4$.
peak at $\delta = 13.1$: $\text{COOH}$ / carboxylic acid proton.

hints: Recall what happens to $\text{O-H}$ and $\text{N-H}$ protons when $\text{D}_2\text{O}$ is added, think about exchange and visibility in proton NMR.
walkthrough:
Spot the exchangeable proton**
The $\text{COOH}$ proton is labile and acidic. In $\text{D}_2\text{O}$ it rapidly exchanges: $\text{RCOOH} + \text{D}_2\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{RCOOD} + \text{HOD}$. Deuterium does not resonate in proton NMR, so the signal at $\delta$ 13.1 vanishes.
Final answer: Peak at $\delta$ 13.1 / $\text{COOH}$ peak disappears as the acidic proton exchanges with deuterium / D from $\text{D}_2\text{O}$.

hints: Look at what is lost when two adjacent $\text{COOH}$ groups form the cyclic anhydride K on heating, count the atoms removed.
walkthrough:
See water leaving**
Two $\text{-COOH}$ groups on neighbouring carbons join together with loss of $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ to give the five membered cyclic anhydride K. Removing water by heat is dehydration, also described as intramolecular condensation or elimination.
Final answer: Dehydration / elimination / (auto)condensation (to form an anhydride).
